description.summary: A yōkai of Japanese coastal folklore most strongly associated with the Shimane Peninsula in former Izumo Province: a colossal, fleshless whale skeleton that surfaces from the sea on rainy nights surrounded by strange birds and fish, and brings curses, fire, and pestilence upon the whaling villages it visits.
description.full: Bake-kujira (化け鯨, 'ghost whale' or 'changed whale') is a yōkai of Japanese coastal folklore. It is most strongly attested in the Shimane Peninsula of former Izumo Province (modern north-eastern Shimane Prefecture), historically a major whaling region known as the 'Sea of Whales'. Folkloric accounts describe a vast, fleshless whale skeleton (sometimes specified as a baleen whale) that surfaces near a whaling village on a rainy or misty night, accompanied by schools of unfamiliar fish and unfamiliar dark birds. When fishermen attempt to harpoon it, their weapons pass harmlessly through the gaps between its bones. The villages it visits are subsequently afflicted with fires, plagues, famine, or other misfortunes. Notably, Bake-kujira is poorly attested in surviving Edo-period yōkai compendia and ukiyo-e — the modern prominence of the figure largely derives from the 20th-century manga artist and yōkai scholar Mizuki Shigeru (水木しげる), who featured Bake-kujira in his GeGeGe no Kitarō comics and yōkai encyclopaedias. Mizuki himself reportedly fell ill while working on a kamishibai (paper-theatre) Bake-kujira project in the 1950s, an event he later described in interviews. Local Oki and Izumo whale traditions — including kabuki performances and Buddhist memorial rites for whales — frame Bake-kujira within a wider Japanese folk understanding of the spiritual debt owed to whales taken by whaling communities.

etymology.origin: Japanese 化け (bake, from bakeru, 'to transform / become a ghost') + 鯨 (kujira, 'whale').
etymology.meaning: 'Transformed whale' — i.e. a whale that has become a yōkai. Sometimes also 'ghost whale'.
etymology.first_use: The name and figure are most reliably documented from 20th-century yōkai literature; the underlying coastal whale-spirit tradition predates the modern label.

taxonomy.variant: Shimane / Izumo coastal tradition; Mizuki Shigeru 20th-century redaction

features.description: Described as the bare skeleton of a great baleen whale, with no flesh or skin.
Harpoons and weapons pass harmlessly through the gaps in the bones.
Surrounded by schools of unfamiliar fish, sometimes in unusual species combinations.
Surrounded by unusual dark birds wheeling above the water.
Sightings are placed on misty, rainy nights near whaling villages.

physical.morphology: A spectral whale skeleton — visually like a stranded baleen whale's bones, but appearing on the open water and accompanied by uncanny faunal escorts.

abilities.description: Harpoons pass through it without effect.
Visits curse villages with fires, epidemics, famine, and misfortune.
Attracts unfamiliar fish and dark birds in its presence.

habitat_preference: coastal waters off the Shimane Peninsula
patterns: Appears at night, in rain or mist

range.description: Strongly associated with the Shimane Peninsula and Oki Islands of former Izumo Province (modern Shimane Prefecture), Japan. Modern depictions, popularised through Mizuki Shigeru's manga, have spread the figure into nation-wide and global popular culture.
regions: former whaling villages of western Japan

hotspots.name: Shimane Peninsula

location.description: Coastal Shimane Peninsula, former Izumo Province

hotspots.notes: Core region of the Bake-kujira tradition.

hotspots.name: Oki Islands

location.description: Oki Islands, off the Shimane coast

hotspots.notes: Whaling villages in the Oki area maintain traditions of whale memorial rites and kabuki performances; a 1764 Chibu Bay whale stranding is sometimes cited in this context.

first_recorded.source: Coastal oral tradition; specific Edo-period printed records of the named figure are scarce. Modern prominence is anchored by Mizuki Shigeru's 20th-century work.

peak_activity_periods.description: Whaling industries flourish along the Sea of Japan; coastal whale-spirit folklore proliferates orally.
Mizuki Shigeru popularises Bake-kujira through kamishibai, manga (GeGeGe no Kitarō), and yōkai encyclopaedias.

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Reported in association with rainy and misty coastal weather rather than a specific season.

origins.cultural_roots: Japanese coastal whaling communities of western Honshu, especially the Sea of Japan littoral. Embedded in a wider Japanese tradition of memorial rites for whales taken by whalers (kujira-kuyō) and of yōkai associated with the sea.
origins.earliest_accounts: Surviving Edo-period yōkai compendia (e.g. Toriyama Sekien's series) do not include the Bake-kujira; the tradition appears to have circulated orally and to have been popularised in printed form in the 20th century.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to broader Japanese coastal yōkai (umibōzu, funayūrei, isonade) and to whale-memorial Buddhist rites in former whaling regions.

timeline.event: Coastal whaling industries flourish in Izumo and along the Sea of Japan; Bake-kujira tradition circulates orally.
timeline.source: General Edo-period whaling history; secondary scholarship on Japanese coastal folklore.

timeline.event: Mizuki Shigeru reportedly works on a kamishibai (paper-theatre) project featuring Bake-kujira and falls ill with high fever during production.
timeline.significance: Modern reintroduction of the figure into Japanese popular culture.
timeline.source: Mizuki Shigeru's autobiographical writings and interviews.

timeline.event: Mizuki Shigeru includes Bake-kujira in his yōkai encyclopaedias and GeGeGe no Kitarō manga and anime.
timeline.significance: Establishes the figure's modern visual canon.
timeline.source: Mizuki Shigeru, Yōkai daizukai and other yōkai compendia.

history.modern_era: Bake-kujira is now widely recognised in Japan and globally as one of the more visually striking yōkai. It appears in Mizuki Shigeru's manga, in animated GeGeGe no Kitarō adaptations, and in international media including the video game Smite. It has also become an emblem in some recent ecological-allegory readings of yōkai, as an embodiment of cetacean revenge for overharvesting.

documentary.name: Mizuki Shigeru — yōkai compendia and GeGeGe no Kitarō
documentary.description: Mizuki Shigeru's drawings and short prose entries on Bake-kujira are the principal modern documentary record of the creature.
documentary.analysis: Mizuki Shigeru's work synthesises older oral tradition with his own visual designs.
documentary.source: Mizuki Shigeru, Zoku Yōkai Daizukai and other yōkai compendia.

paranormal.name: Vengeful whale spirit
paranormal.description: Within Japanese coastal tradition, Bake-kujira is read as the spirit of a slain whale (or whales) taking revenge on the whaling communities. This reading is reinforced by Buddhist and folk practices of whale memorial rites (kujira-kuyō).
evidence_cited: Buddhist whale-memorial rites in former whaling villages

scientific.name: Whale stranding folklore
scientific.description: Some scholars suggest the tradition reflects awe and dread occasioned by occasional mass whale strandings or by the appearance of decomposing whale carcasses at sea — striking, foul-smelling, and visually skeletal.
proponents: Folklore scholars on Japanese coastal yōkai
evidence_cited: Japanese whaling history; documented mass strandings in the Sea of Japan

skeptical.name: Modern yōkai construction
skeptical.description: Bake-kujira's modern prominence is largely the product of Mizuki Shigeru's 20th-century work; older Edo yōkai compendia do not depict it, suggesting the canonical visual figure is a modern crystallisation of older oral coastal folklore.
proponents: Folklore scholars (e.g. yōkai-studies tradition following Komatsu Kazuhiko)
evidence_cited: Absence of Bake-kujira in surviving Edo yōkai prints
Documented role of Mizuki Shigeru in popularising the figure

folklore.beliefs: Treats Bake-kujira as a vengeful spirit warning against the spiritual consequences of unchecked whaling; embedded in Japanese whale-memorial rites.
